Pullman Strike · 1894

Whose Account Do You Trust?

Investigate what contributed to the Pullman Strike. Build a claim, compare accounts, and bring your revised interpretation to the seminar.

Source trail

15–20 minutes · Work at your own pace

Evidence workspace

1 of 4 accounts available

Jump to your response

In 1894, Pullman employees near Chicago struck after wage cuts during an economic downturn. Many rented homes in the company town.

Historical background
  • The Pullman Company made railroad sleeping cars near Chicago and ran a company town where many workers rented homes.
  • During the economic downturn of the 1890s, wages were cut. Workers argued that rent and other living costs did not fall as much as wages.
  • Workers went on strike in 1894. The American Railway Union backed them with a wider boycott involving trains carrying Pullman cars.
  • Rail traffic was disrupted. Federal intervention and court action became major parts of the conflict. Violence occurred in some locations during the broader strike and boycott.
  • Historical interpretations differ over responsibility, federal power, workers’ demands, union strategy, and what the conflict meant.

Company town: A town run by a company. Boycott: An organized refusal to deal with something as a form of protest.

Worker’s account

Simulated composite for learning

A private letter to a sibling

Readable transcript

Dear Brother, I ought to tell you how things stand here. My wages have been cut, and the rent is still as hard to meet. If I lose more days at the shops, I do not know how we shall manage for groceries.

When we take our complaints to the foremen, they give us little hearing. I had hoped to keep at work, for we cannot well do without the pay. It seems to me we have come to a strike because we could see no other way.

Source context
Form, audience, and purpose
A private letter to a sibling describing the worker’s situation and concerns.
Access to events
The writer knows the household’s finances firsthand and has limited knowledge of company-wide finances or negotiations.

Company statement

Simulated composite for learning

A statement for distribution to newspapers

Readable transcript

Statement for the Press

The company wishes to make clear the circumstances under which wages were reduced. The falling demand for cars has diminished our receipts. The reduction in wages was necessary, in the company’s judgment, to keep the works in operation.

The letting of houses is a separate matter from the wages paid at the works. In considering the complaints now made, it is proper to bear in mind the sums the company has already spent upon dwellings and facilities for the town.

Source context
Form, audience, and purpose
A public statement distributed to newspapers to defend company decisions.
Access to events
It presents the company’s own decisions and explanations. It may contain useful information about operations and is also meant to persuade.

Newspaper account

Simulated composite for learning

A Chicago newspaper report

Readable transcript

Railway Traffic Delayed

Railway traffic was delayed, and crowds gathered near the yards. Passengers waiting for trains spoke with impatience of the interruption to their journeys.

A railroad manager laid responsibility for the delays upon the leaders of the union. Complaints of reduced wages were also reported among the Pullman men.

Source context
Form, audience, and purpose
A newspaper report for a citywide readership, rather than primarily Pullman workers. It reports on rail disruptions.
Access to events
The reporter observes some events firsthand and relies heavily on railroad officials. The claim about union leaders comes from a railroad manager.

Reform investigator’s account

Simulated composite for learning

An investigator’s field notes

Readable transcript

Notes on Living Conditions

Spoke with several families in the company town. In the small dwellings I visited, I made note of household expenses and of what the families said about managing them. The arrangement raises a question as to how much independence a family has when its home and its work depend upon the same company.

Some residents spoke well of the town’s cleanliness and of the services provided. I set down their remarks alongside the observations on housing and household expenses.

Source context
Form, audience, and purpose
Field notes by an investigator sympathetic to reform who seeks evidence about living conditions. The materials do not specify an audience.
Access to events
The notes draw on observations and interviews with several families. They are not a representative survey.

Check your comparison

The public purpose of the Company statement does not rule out useful information about company decisions. The Worker’s account offers a firsthand view of household pressures. The Newspaper account combines observation with a railroad manager’s explanation.

Corroborate means to check a claim against other evidence. If the Company statement and Newspaper account agree, consider where each got its information before counting the agreement as independent support.

Check what the field notes can support

The Reform investigator’s account gives evidence from several families and includes differing views of town services. It can help you compare household pressures with the Worker’s account. Several interviews cannot establish what every family experienced.
